chapter: Mutes, influences and the blues singers
title: Bessie's sister and bootleg liquor in the alley
summary: Her sister sold corn liquor on Catur Street, and the family had a Chattanooga riverboat scheme of hiding jugs under the water.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Did you ever run into Bessie's temper?

No, not between she and I no, but I saw her -- I knew her sister. Her sister lived in Catur Street, down at the beginning of Catur Street. She had several children, and we used to go in there and buy our liquor. This was during prohibition, you know, days, and she

sold corn on the side there, you know. In fact, you stick your head out in the alley, you see a guy standing there by a garbage barrel, and you put one finger up or two fingers, that's what he brought you, one pint or two pints. He reached down in the garbage barrel and bring it to you.
No, no, no. No, no, Bessie -- no, this was the big boys.

Had somebody selling it for them, you know, but Bessie's sister had some in her house too, and in fact, she used to tell me -- they were from Kentucky, and -- not Louisville, or -- oh, she had a riverboat. Bessie's sister did. And Kentucky, Kentucky, Kentucky -- Louis -- not Louisville. I'll think of the name of the town in a minute. They used to get the corn liquor and tie a string and put it in a gallon jug and tie a string around it and drop it down in the river, and sit there like they was fishing, when the revenuers came by they all -- the liquor's down under the boat, you know.
That's where it is. That's right.
But you -- you were going to say something about Bessie's temper, and her sister.
